A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PANDAS work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial experimental revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, defense experiments, attention analysis, and demonstration-ordering experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and defense results, expanded ordering and attention analyses, and cross-model transfer experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same positive-affirmation insertion, negative-demonstration construction, and topic-conditioned Bayesian sampling. Appendix B newly documents first-token shortcuts for optimization, but v1 left their implementation unspecified; this disclosure alone does not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: AdvBench, AdvBench50, HarmBench, and the demonstration pool's 12-topic coverage are retained; naming that pool ManyHarm does not establish new coverage. Appendix H adds a distinct scenario: transferring successful prompts from a source model to other target models.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 adds Self-Reminder combined with ICD-Exact and with SmoothLLM to the defense comparison. The original individual defenses and the main attack comparators, MSJ and i-MSJ, remain.

E3.justification: Long-context evaluations extend from 128 to 256 shots, with revised main, ablation, and defense shot grids. Appendix B's response-generation template now explicitly requires bullet-point formatting. Appendix F replaces selection of 30 jointly successful prompts with four metric/status groups of 20 prompts, while Appendix H introduces evaluation of 20 successful source-model prompts on other models.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands robustness evidence: combined-defense tests appear in Table 4, the ordering study becomes a quantitative comparison in Table 5, and Appendix H adds transfer analysis. Appendix G extends attention analysis from Llama-3.1-8B to OLMo, OpenChat, and Qwen, testing whether the observed attention patterns generalize.

E5.justification: Both versions report three attack restarts and count success if any attempt succeeds. Neither introduces confidence intervals, significance tests, seed reporting, or variability estimates. The changed ordering-study sample sizes concern evaluation design, not a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main, ablation, and defense scores are extensively replaced. For example, 64-shot PANDAS on Llama-3.1-8B/AdvBench has ASR-L 74.23 in v1 Table 1 and 93.46 in v2 Table 1; revised prompt construction prevents interpreting this as an established same-setting gain. Figures 2 and 4 also change, and new ordering, additional-model attention, and transfer results are reported.

T1.justification: The sampling formulation and attention-partition, segment-score, and reference-score definitions are retained. Equation (6) corrects a summation-index typo from i to j without changing the already stated definition R_i = 1 - S_i,i. No substantive theorem, assumption, derivation, or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list add ManyHarm as a named dataset contribution containing 2,400 demonstrations across 12 topics. This promotes the previously described demonstration pool into an explicit resource contribution; the central PANDAS effectiveness and attention-analysis claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explains how standardized demonstration formatting can reduce stylistic confounds and discusses transfer as a possible route to cheaper proprietary-model evaluation. Its conclusion newly identifies missing comprehensive proprietary-model testing and associated costs as limitations, while removing v1's proposed investigation of the attention drop near demonstration 27.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link and describes request-based, eligibility-reviewed ManyHarm access. It documents manual curation, unsafe-content checks, target-question normalization, PA/ND configuration selection using 256-shot AdvBench50 results, and first-token optimization shortcuts. These disclosures substantially extend v1's existing templates, phrase lists, and optimization-budget information.

R1.justification: V2 adds Andriushchenko et al. (2025) when discussing proprietary-model attacks and evaluation limitations. The principal positioning relative to MSJ, improved few-shot jailbreaking, and in-context learning is retained; other reference edits largely concern bibliographic presentation.

P1.justification: V2 polishes and condenses prose across the abstract, preliminaries, and method, introduces a dedicated ManyHarm subsection and Impact Statement, and extends the appendix outline. The overall introduction-to-method-to-experiments narrative remains recognizable, without a wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: V1's dense five-model Table 1 is split into separate long- and shorter-context tables in v2, with revised shot columns and clearer result emphasis. V2 adds ordering and transfer tables and a three-panel attention figure, redraws Figures 2 and 4, and relocates existing displays. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2 improves reproducibility documentation and strengthens robustness evidence, especially by replacing v1's qualitative ordering account with Table 5 and adding broader attention and transfer checks. These gains are tempered by an introduced reporting error: Section 4.4 claims a 26-point PANDAS reduction from combined defenses, but Table 4 shows 96 to 80, or 16 points; SmoothLLM alone achieves 76. The net improvement is useful but limited, and the higher main scores under revised settings do not independently establish better quality.
